Threat.value: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard

Memory.value: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.
Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Negative Appraisals.value: I can't stop bad things from happening to me
I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
I was betrayed by someone I trusted

issues.explanation: Fire/flames is not a plausible primary trigger for childhood physical abuse by a caregiver unless other profile elements indicate fire-related abuse or a fire context, which they do not. The rest of the trigger, threat, memory, and appraisal items point to interpersonal threat rather than burn/fire trauma, so this item is hard to reconcile with the trauma type.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Survival Guilt: I feel guilty for surviving when others did not
issues.explanation: Survival guilt about others dying is difficult to reconcile with childhood physical abuse by a caregiver when no other items reference deaths, fatalities, or witnessing others die. It also conflicts with the rest of the profile, which centers on helplessness and failure to stop abuse rather than surviving when others did not.

vignette:
Dorothea Hale is a 73-year-old married woman of European descent who has worked for decades as a QA Engineer, a profession built entirely on the premise that errors can be caught before they cause harm - a premise that, in the most formative years of her life, proved catastrophically false. She came to her first intake appointment neatly dressed, her speech measured and precise, and she spent the first twenty minutes of the session describing her childhood home in procedural terms, as though she were documenting a defect log rather than a life.

The abuse began when Dorothea was approximately six years old and continued until she left for college at eighteen. Her father, the primary caregiver in the household following her mother's early illness, was physically violent in a way that was both unpredictable and methodical. There were no reliable warnings. A misplaced cup, a hesitation in answering a question, a shadow falling across the kitchen doorway at the wrong angle - any of these could precede the violence. What Dorothea remembered most vividly, and what she described in the flat, halting language of someone reading from a document they did not write, was the particular quality of his movements: the sudden turn from the counter, the fast reach across the table, the way a raised arm could resolve into anything or nothing. She said she remembered these moments the way you remember photographs - each one precise, lit from a fixed angle, utterly still. She could describe the pattern of the linoleum, the colour of the light through the kitchen window. What she could not do, she said quietly, was find any words for what those images meant to her. She knew what had happened. The knowledge sat in her like a stone. But when she tried to speak around it, the language simply was not there.

For most of her adult life, Dorothea managed. She married a gentle, soft-spoken man named Robert, built a career, raised two children. But she organised her world around certain rules that had formed so gradually she had barely noticed them solidifying. She did not attend funerals. When her mother-in-law died eleven years ago, she sent flowers and stayed home, and Robert had not pressed her, though something between them shifted quietly in the weeks that followed. When her closest colleague retired last spring and the team held a small memorial gathering for another coworker who had passed, Dorothea found a reason to work from home that day. At work - where she is one of the few senior engineers who still comes into the office several days a week - she had arranged her desk so that her back was never to the door. When a junior male colleague leaned suddenly across her workstation to point at her monitor, she was out of her chair before she had processed what had happened, her heart already loud, her hands already cold. She had come to believe this was simply how her body worked: it knew danger before she did, and the knowing was not a thought but a movement.

What frightened Dorothea most, in the abstract, was uncertainty itself - any situation in which she could not predict the outcome. This made her exceptionally good at her job, where the systematic elimination of unknowns was the entire point. It made other parts of her life considerably harder. She had come to believe, with a conviction she described as absolute, that she had never done enough to protect herself as a child, and that this failure of action was something she would carry permanently. She was equally certain that the person who should have kept her safe had instead been the source of harm, and that this fact said something definitive about the reliability of the world. She did not use the word betrayal. She used the phrase "I learned early not to expect protection."

What finally brought Dorothea to seek help was a diagnosis - not hers, but Robert's. A serious illness, uncertain in its trajectory. She told the intake clinician that she could feel herself becoming someone she did not want to be around him: watchful, remote, occasionally numb in a way she recognised as old and familiar. She was not sure what she hoped for from therapy. What she was most afraid of, she said, was that she would not be able to find the words even if she tried.
